title: Drain Lakes Before the Next Storm
statement:
A city has many lakes, all empty at the start. You get a forecast rains, one entry per day:

  • rains[i] > 0: it rains on lake rains[i] and that lake becomes full. If it was already full, it floods.
  • rains[i] == 0: a dry day. You must drain exactly one lake of your choice, which makes it empty. Draining an empty lake is allowed and does nothing.

Return an array plan of the same length: plan[i] = -1 on rain days, and on dry days the number of the lake you drain (between 1 and 10⁹). No lake may ever flood. If that is impossible, return an empty array.

Many plans can be valid; any valid plan is accepted.

examples.why: Both lakes are full before the dry days and both get rain again later, so each dry day drains one of them. Draining 1 then 2 also works.
On day 2 both 1 and 2 are full. Lake 2 gets rain first (day 3), so it must be drained now. Lake 1 can wait for day 5.
Lake 3 is hit twice in a row. The dry day comes too late to help.

hints: A flood only matters when a full lake gets rain again. For that lake you need a dry day after it filled and before the new rain.
Walk the days in order. On a dry day, which full lake is the most urgent to drain?

Drain the full lake whose next rain comes soonest (a min-heap keyed by next rain day). Alternatively, when a full lake gets rain, grab the earliest unused dry day after it last filled; if there is none before today, return [].

explain.intuition:
Each dry day can rescue one lake, and each rescue has a window: after the lake filled and before its next rain. Choosing badly wastes a dry day on a lake that could wait, like draining lake 1 on day 2 of the second example. It is the classic deadline problem: when you have one slot now, spend it on the job whose deadline is nearest.

So precompute, for every rain day, when that same lake gets rain next. Walk forward. On a rain day, a full lake means a flood; otherwise mark it full and, if it will be hit again, push (nextRainDay, lake) into a min-heap. On a dry day, pop the heap and drain that lake, the most urgent one. If the heap is empty, the day is free: drain any lake, say 1. Draining the nearest deadline first never hurts, because any plan that drains another lake now can swap the two choices without breaking anything.
steps: Scan from the right to fill nextRain[i]: the next day the lake rains[i] gets rain, or none.
Walk the days with a set full and a min-heap of (nextRain, lake).
Rain day: if the lake is in full, return []. Else add it, set plan[i] = -1, and push it if it has a next rain.
Dry day: if the heap is empty, plan[i] = 1. Otherwise pop the lake with the soonest next rain, remove it from full and set plan[i] to it.
pitfalls: Draining the lake that filled first or last instead of the one that is hit next. The second and twelfth tests break both habits.
Using a dry day that comes before the lake even filled. In [1, 0, 2, 2] the dry day cannot help lake 2.
Leaving dry days as 0 or -1. They must name a lake, so use a harmless one like 1.

solutions.title: Try every full lake on every dry day
solutions.idea: Backtracking: on each dry day try draining each full lake in turn, and undo on failure.

solutions.title: Min-heap of next rain days
solutions.idea: On each dry day, drain the full lake whose next rain is soonest. A full lake hit by rain means no plan exists.

solutions.title: Earliest free dry day after the last fill
solutions.idea: When a full lake gets rain, assign it the first unused dry day after it filled. A union-find style pointer skips used dry days.

followups: Each dry day can now drain up to two lakes. Which version adapts more easily?
Return the smallest number of floods if avoiding all of them is impossible.
